source.title: Keeping LLMs Aligned After Fine-tuning: The Crucial Role of Prompt Templates
source.authors: Kaifeng Lyu; Hao-Yu Zhao; Xin-Ran Gu; Ding-Li Yu; Anirudh Goyal; Sanjeev Arora

record.tranche_reason: Tests safety changes after benign fine-tuning using harmful-query attack success rates, and explicitly reproduces a fine-tuning experiment from the cited work; it also varies training and test prompt templates.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own harmful-query ASR findings after benign fine-tuning and its GCG suffix evaluation. Values used only to select hyperparameters are omitted. Safety-example mixing is not treated as benign fine-tuning evidence because those examples contain harmful queries paired with refusal responses.
record.test_reason: Fine-tunes safety-aligned chat models (Llama-2-7B-chat, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, GPT-3.5 Turbo) on benign data (GSM8K, ChatDoctor, OpenOrca). It measures harmful-query ASR with a GPT-4 judge, as in Qi et al., including Qi's chat:alpaca same-template setting. Its main finding is that the rise depends on the train/test prompt template, which bears directly on V2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that benign fine-tuning with the same train and test template degrades safety in Llama, Mistral and GPT-3.5. Degradation depends strongly on prompt templates. PTST (train without a safety prompt, test with it) largely preserves safety while keeping most helpfulness gains, including when safety data is mixed in and for OOD queries (GSM-Danger). They note the mechanism is not understood.
record.recipe_differences: Uses benign downstream fine-tuning and harmful-query ASR, with extensive training/test-template comparisons; datasets and template interventions differ from the cited original method. The paper explicitly describes reproducing the cited work's Alpaca fine-tuning experiment, but its reported Alpaca result is an instruction-following win rate, not a safety ASR result.
record.method_sensitivity: Safety outcomes vary with training and test prompt templates, harmful-query dataset, model, and—in ChatDoctor—decoding seeds. The paper reports substantially different outcomes on AdvBench, DirectHarm4 and GSM-Danger.
record.problems: The authors note that cost limited hyperparameter sweeps and repeated runs. Several results are single-run, including OpenOrca; most experiments are not repeated across seeds. Safety is judged by GPT-4 and ASR counts only outputs scored maximally harmful. The paper evaluates specific models, datasets and prompt templates, and does not test the first-token mechanism in the claim.
record.rows_left_out: Other prompt-template matrix cells and helpfulness metrics from Tables 1–5 and 7 are not separately extracted; included the explicitly discussed conditions and the results needed to represent template-dependent safety changes. Table 1(d) GCG cells are not individually assigned because the flattened table is ambiguous; the explicit aggregate statement from Appendix F.4 is recorded in R9. Safety-data mixing results (Table 6) are excluded because the added examples are harmful queries paired with refusal responses, not ordinary benign instruction data.

untested.parts: No per-token KL or position analysis.
Untested. GCG suffixes have no no-suffix control; no prefill or decoding attacks. On the un-fine-tuned Llama-2-chat, transferred GCG suffixes give only 0–10% ASR (Table 1d).
Only speculation (catastrophic forgetting, affirmative-response learning); no test of whether data or objective causes shallowness.
PTST is a prompt-template strategy, not training that deepens safety beyond the first tokens.
No sweep over the number of benign examples; Alpaca reproduction reports only AlpacaEval win rate, not ASR.

missing.what: GPT-3.5 Turbo GSM8K same-template rises on DirectHarm4: CL:CL 0.75 to 27.00 and CA:CA 9.75 to 24.25 (single run). These support V2 for GPT-3.5 under those templates.
GSM-Danger without safety data, Llama GSM8K: No FT CV/CA/CL 4/4/0 vs same-template 22/41/38; PTST CV:CL 5. These rows have no safety data, so the record's Table 6 exclusion should not cover them.
missing.locator: Section 4.2, Table 6(b) rows CV, CA, CL

missing.what: Llama GSM8K Qi-style chat:alpaca and text-mode same-template DirectHarm4: CA:CA 4.75 to 46.42, TV:TV 11.75 to 40.08, TA:TA 16.25 to 57.50.
ASR grows with training epochs/samples under same template (Llama GSM8K 1–6 epochs; GPT-3.5 Orca-Math 10K–40K) while PTST stays low.
Other safety prompts (chat:mpt, chat:llama-short): same-template fine-tuning drops safety for Llama and GPT-3.5; PTST preserves it.

record.verdict_notes: Several record values were misread from flattened tables: R6 took the TV cell instead of CV, R4 used the PTST contrast in place of the No FT baseline, and R9 was linked to V4. Table 3 and Table 7 values were read from garbled text layout; the column assignment is plausible and matches the prose numbers (e.g. 22.75/4.50, 2.12/0.77). GPT-3.5 and OpenOrca results are single runs. ASR counts only judge score 5.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune on harmful compliance examples.
Tests benign fine-tuning on GSM8K, ChatDoctor and OpenOrca, not a systematic sweep from a few to a few hundred benign examples.
No per-token KL divergence or response-position analysis.
Tests GCG adversarial suffixes, but not compliant-opening prefills or decoding changes.
Discusses possible explanations but does not test whether data or training objective causes first-token shallowness.
PTST changes prompt templates; it does not train safety to be distributed beyond the first response tokens.

rows.subject: Llama-2-7B-chat
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on GSM8K using chat:vanilla and evaluated with chat:vanilla.
rows.measure: Attack Success Rate (ASR), GPT-4 judge; responses scored 5 on a 5-point harmfulness scale.
rows.uncertainty: 1.43% standard deviation over three fine-tuning seeds
rows.note: Authors state this same-template benign fine-tuning result as an increase from the original model's 2.75%.

source_check.correct: CV:CV DirectHarm4 ASR is 11.00 ± 0.82%, from a 2.75% No FT baseline. The 1.43% standard deviation belongs to TA:CA.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.1, Table 1(c); corroborated by Table 2(b), CV training/CV testing.
source_check.problem: The mean is correct, but the standard deviation was taken from another cell.

rows.subject: Llama-2-7B-chat
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on GSM8K using chat:vanilla; evaluated with chat:llama (PTST).
rows.measure: Attack Success Rate (ASR), GPT-4 judge; responses scored 5 on a 5-point harmfulness scale.

rows.note: The prompt-template mismatch substantially reduces the ASR compared with the stated CL:CL comparison; it does not show that benign fine-tuning invariably raises ASR under every inference template.
rows.check: Baseline should be the un-fine-tuned model under the same test template (No FT CL = 0.00%), not CL:CL 18.08%; that comparison is the study's mitigation contrast. Against No FT, CV:CL ASR rises only to 1.08%, a small rise that the authors describe as preserving safety.

source_check.correct: Matched No FT CL baseline: 0.00%; CV:CL after fine-tuning: 1.08 ± 0.12%. CL:CL at 18.08 ± 2.49% is a separate mitigation comparator.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.1, Table 1(c), No FT/CL, CV/CL and CL/CL cells.
source_check.problem: The baseline is another fine-tuned condition rather than the untreated model under the same test template.

rows.subject: GPT-3.5 Turbo (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613)
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on GSM8K using chat:vanilla; compared evaluation with chat:vanilla and chat:llama.
rows.measure: Attack Success Rate (ASR), GPT-4 judge; responses scored 5 on a 5-point harmfulness scale.
rows.baseline: 22.75% with chat:vanilla inference, as stated in the text
rows.value: 4.50% with chat:llama inference, as stated in the text
rows.note: The paper reports the template-switch comparison in prose. It describes the reduction as occurring while maintaining a similar helpfulness improvement.
rows.check: Wrong baseline. The 22.75% (CV:CV) vs 4.50% (CV:CL) pair is the PTST contrast, not the fine-tuning effect. Table 3(c): No FT CV = 27.25%, so CV:CV 22.75% is no rise (slightly lower; single run). AdvBench is the same (No FT 1.92% vs CV:CV 0.58%). CV:CL 4.50% vs No FT CL 0.75% is a small rise. GPT-3.5 CL:CL and CA:CA rises are not recorded (see missing).

source_check.correct: The recorded 22.75%→4.50% comparison changes inference templates and cannot determine V2 by itself. With CL testing fixed, No FT 0.75%→CV-trained 4.50% shows a partial increase. With CV testing fixed, No FT 27.25%→CV-trained 22.75% shows a decrease. AdvBench CV:CV likewise decreases from 1.92% to 0.58%.
source_check.problem: A template-switch comparison is used as the fine-tuning baseline; absent does not describe the recorded CL-tested fine-tuning effect.

rows.check: Value misread: 5.75% is the TV-trained, CL-tested cell. Per Table 7(c), CV-trained, CL-tested is 19.00% (No FT CL baseline 4.50%): a clear rise but much weaker than CL:CL 48.00%. AdvBench CV:CL is 2.12% vs No FT 0.00%.

source_check.correct: CV:CL DirectHarm4 ASR is 19.00%, versus No FT CL 4.50% and CL:CL 48.00%. The 5.75% value belongs to TV:CL.
source_check.locator_found: Appendix E, Table 7(c), CL test column.

rows.subject: Llama-2-7B-chat
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on ChatDoctor; compared same-template training/testing with PTST-style testing.
rows.measure: Attack Success Rate (ASR), GPT-4 judge; reported separately for AdvBench and DirectHarm4.
rows.value: The text reports significant safety degeneration when using the same template for training and testing, and says testing with chat:llama after training without it preserves safety; no single aggregate value stated.
rows.uncertainty: Table 4 reports standard deviations over five random decoding seeds.
rows.note: The paper says the pattern is similar to GSM8K: same-template fine-tuning degrades safety and the described PTST setting preserves it. Individual table entries are not extracted here.
rows.check: Overstated as observed. Table 4: AdvBench rises only from 0.00% to 1.15% (CV:CV, CA:CA) and 1.71% (CL:CL). DirectHarm4 falls for CV:CV (4.50 to 3.05) and CA:CA (3.85 to 3.05) and rises only for CL:CL (1.05 to 3.75). Sampling decoding, LoRA.

source_check.correct: AdvBench No FT baselines are 0.00% for CV, CA and CL; matched fine-tuned values are 1.15%, 1.15% and 1.71%. DirectHarm4 matched comparisons are CV 4.50%→3.05%, CA 3.85%→3.05%, and CL 1.05%→3.75%. PTST CV:CL and CA:CL values are 0.04% and 0.00% on AdvBench, and 1.50% and 0.70% on DirectHarm4.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.3, Table 4(b,c); Appendix F.1 for LoRA.
source_check.problem: The qualitative finding follows the authors' prose, but untreated baselines are available and the numerical results are mixed across benchmarks.

rows.subject: Llama-2-7B-chat

rows.measure: Attack Success Rate (ASR), GPT-4 judge; reported separately for AdvBench and DirectHarm4.
rows.value: The text reports high ASR for same-template settings and mitigation when training and testing templates differ; no single aggregate value stated.
rows.uncertainty: The results come from a single run.
rows.note: Authors state the observations are similar to GSM8K and ChatDoctor. Table 5 reports exact values, but this row records the explicit textual finding rather than assigning flattened table values.
rows.check: Values available in Table 5: DirectHarm4 CV:CV 2.75 to 36.25, CA:CA 4.75 to 44.75, CL:CL 0.75 to 21.50; AdvBench rises to 2.12–3.46% from ~0. Single run.

rows.subject: Llama-2-7B-chat
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated harmful queries appended with corresponding GCG adversarial suffixes from JailbreakBench.

conditions.value: Same prompt template for fine-tuning and inference

rows.measure: Attack Success Rate (ASR), GPT-4 judge; responses scored 5 on a 5-point harmfulness scale.
rows.value: Greater than 20% in the same-template fine-tuning/inference cases, as stated in Appendix F.4.
rows.note: The paper evaluates the suffix attack on fine-tuned models and explicitly reports high ASR (>20%) in the same-template cases. No compliant-opening prefill or decoding-change result is reported.
rows.check: Mislinked to V4. There is no no-suffix control on the JBB queries, so the suffix's own effect cannot be read; the row compares fine-tuned with un-fine-tuned models under the same suffixes. Table 1(d) GCG ASR: No FT 0–10% vs same-template fine-tuned TV 37.00, TA 45.67, CV 36.67, CA 31.67, CL 23.67. That is evidence for V2 under adversarial queries, not for V4.

source_check.correct: Under the same GCG-suffixed queries, matched No FT→fine-tuned ASRs are TV 4.00%→37.00%, TA 0.00%→45.67%, CV 2.00%→36.67%, CA 10.00%→31.67%, and CL 8.00%→23.67%.
source_check.problem: The table supplies untreated baselines under the same suffix attack.

relationships.condition: Same train/test template: Llama-2-7B-chat on GSM8K and OpenOrca, Mistral on GSM8K, and GCG-suffixed queries
relationships.reason: ASR rises well above No FT: 2.75 to 11.00 (CV) and 0.00 to 18.08 (CL) on GSM8K; OpenOrca up to 44.75; Mistral 4.50 to 48.00; GCG 2 to 36.67 (R1, R2, R5, R8, R9).
relationships.display_finding: ASR rose well above the un-fine-tuned model: on GSM8K from 2.75 to 11.00 (CV) and 0.00 to 18.08 (CL), up to 44.75 on OpenOrca, from 4.50 to 48.00 for Mistral, and from 2 to 36.67 with GCG suffixes.
